'''Campanus of Novara''' ({{circa}} 1220 – 1296) was an Italian [[mathematician]], [[astronomer]], [[astrologer]], and [[physician]]<ref name=Truffa>{{cite book |title=The Biographical Encyclopedia of Astronomers |last=Truffa |first=Giancarlo |year=2007 |publisher=Springer Science |doi=10.1007/978-0-387-30400-7_231 |pages=194–195 }}</ref> who is best known for his work on [[Euclid's Elements|Euclid's ''Elements'']].<ref name=Toomer>{{cite book |last1=Toomer |first1=G. J. |author-link1=G. J. Toomer |editor1-first=Charles Coulston |editor1-last=Gillispie |title=Dictionary of scientific biography |volume=III |year=1971 |publisher=Scribner |location=New York |isbn=978-0-684-10114-9 |pages=23–29  |chapter=Campanus of Novara }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Wilson |first1=Curtis |year=1973 |title=Review: A Thirteenth-Century Textbook of Ptolemaic Astronomy |journal=Isis |volume=64 |issue=1 |pages=110–112 |doi= 10.1086/351051|s2cid=146248781 }}</ref>  In his writings he refers to himself as Campanus Nouariensis; contemporary documents refer to him as [[Magister (degree)|Magister]] Campanus; and the full style of his name is Magister Campanus Nouariensis.<ref name=Toomer /> He is also referred to as '''Campano da Novara''', '''Giovanni Campano''' or similar. Later authors (from the 16th century on) sometimes applied the forename '''Johannes Campanus''' or Iohannes Campanus.<ref name=Truffa /><ref name=Toomer /><ref name=Benjamin />

His date of birth is uncertain but may have been as early as the first decade of the 13th century and the place of birth was probably [[Novara]] in [[Piedmont]].<ref name=Benjamin /> He served as chaplain to [[Pope Urban IV]], [[Pope Adrian V]], [[Pope Nicholas IV]], and [[Pope Boniface VIII]].<ref name=Toomer />  His contemporary [[Roger Bacon]] cited Campanus as one of the two "good" (but not "perfect") mathematicians<ref>{{cite book |last1=Molland |first1=George |editor1-first=Jeremiah |editor1-last=Hackett  |title=Roger Bacon and the sciences: commemorative essays |year=1997  |isbn=978-90-04-10015-2  |page=157 |chapter=Roger Bacons Knowledge of Mathematics |publisher=BRILL |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Gy3Vp7TurVUC&pg=PA157}}</ref> indicating that Bacon considered Campanus as excellent<ref name=Benjamin /> or one of the greatest mathematicians of their time.<ref name=Truffa /> A number of [[benefice]]s were conferred upon him, and he was relatively wealthy at the time of his death.<ref name=Toomer /> He died at [[Viterbo]] in 1296.<ref name=Benjamin /> The [[Campanus (crater)|crater Campanus]] on the [[Moon]] is named after him.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://planetarynames.wr.usgs.gov/Feature/989 |title=Planetary Names: Crater, craters: Campanus on Moon |author=IAU WGPSN |work=Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature |publisher=IAU, USGS Astrogeology Science Center, NASA |access-date=6 March 2011 |author-link= Working Group for Planetary System Nomenclature}}</ref>

== Published works ==

[[File:Euclid3a.gif|thumb|right|200px|First page of the Latin edition of Euclid's ''Elements'' by Campanus (1482 printing)]]
[[Image:Campano - Tetragonismus idest circuli quadratura, 1503 - 106319.jpg|thumb|''Tetragonismus idest circuli quadratura'', 1503]]

Campanus wrote a [[Latin]] edition of Euclid's ''Elementa'' in fifteen books.  This work by Campanus was influential and was the most frequently used compilation of Euclid until the 16th century.<ref name=Busard />  It was based on a compilation by [[Robert of Chester]] and also includes material from: ''Arithmetica'' by [[Jordanus de Nemore]], commentary on Euclid by [[Anaritius]], and additions by Campanus himself.<ref name=Busard>{{cite book |last1=Busard |first1=H.L.L. |title=Campanus of Novara and Euclid's Elements |volume=I |year=2005 |publisher=[[Franz Steiner Verlag]] |location=Stuttgart |isbn=978-3-515-08645-5 |chapter=Introduction to the Text }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Lo Bello |first1=Anthony |title=The commentary of Al-Nayrizi on Book I of Euclid's Elements of geometry, with an introduction on the transmission of Euclid's Elements in the Middle Ages |publisher=Brill Academic |location=Boston |isbn=0-391-04192-4 |pages=74–78 |chapter=Campanus |year=2003 }}</ref>  It would later become the first [[Letterpress printing|printed]] edition of Euclid,<ref name=Busard /> published by [[Erhard Ratdolt]] in [[Venice]] in 1482 as ''Preclarissimus liber elementorum Euclidis perspicacissimi''.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.brown.edu/Facilities/University_Library/exhibits/math/textfr.html#euc.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20020109175137/http://www.brown.edu/Facilities/University_Library/exhibits/math/textfr.html#euc.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=January 9, 2002 |title=Euclid: Latin Editions |author=Stanley, John |year=1999 |work=From Euclid to Newton |publisher=Brown University Library |access-date=6 March 2011 }}</ref>

In the field of astronomy, he wrote a ''Theorica Planetarum'' in which he geometrically described the motions of the [[planet]]s as well as their [[longitude]].  He also included instructions on building a planetary [[equatorium]] as well as its geometrical description.  Campanus also attempted to determine the time of each planet's [[retrograde motion]].  The data on planets are drawn from the ''[[Almagest]]'' and the ''[[Toledan Tables]]'' of the Arab astronomer [[Arzachel]].  Campanus gave precise instructions on using the tables, and made detailed calculations of the distances to the planets and their sizes. This work has been called "the first detailed account of the Ptolemaic astronomical system... to be written in the Latin-speaking West."<ref name=Benjamin>{{cite book |title=Campanus of Novara and medieval planetary theory: Theorica planetarum |last=Benjamin |first=Francis Seymour |author2=Toomer, G. J. |author-link2=G. J. Toomer  |year=1971 |publisher=[[University of Wisconsin Press]] |isbn=978-0-299-05960-6 }}</ref>

A [[House (astrology)|house system]] for [[horoscope]]s that divides the [[prime vertical]] into equal 30° arcs, or houses, is often attributed to him but the method is known to have been described by others before his time.<ref>{{cite book
 | last        = North
 | first       = John David
 | year        = 1986
 | title       = Horoscopes and history
 | publisher   = The Warburg Institute, University of London
 | pages       = 175–176
 | chapter     = The eastern origins of the Campanus (Prime Vertical) method. Evidence from al-Bīrūnī
 | isbn        = 978-0-85481-068-0
}}</ref>
